utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. I only have one brief comment. I know sometimes in the courtroom strong statements are made by all sides, and I think most of the time, respectfully, we submit, that I think the Prosecution states a truthful and correct position, often forcefully. I do owe, however, the Defence at least a partial apology concerning some documents yesterday. Some of the maps we found had been provided to us. Not all of them. We did not have all the documents that were used yesterday by Defence counsel, including, for example, the HVO organisational chart that was used. But some of the maps, like the 1992 maps and that sort of thing that -- apparently had been provided to us, and so to that extent, I give my apology to the Defence for saying we had not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, I don't know if you have received this. Five minutes before the start of trial for today, we received this big binder, which quite obviously the Prosecution intends to use in the cross-examination. For me to become acquainted with all the documents contained in this binder, I would need at least two hours. They are documents which were never used in this courtroom before, nor were they ever proposed and put forward as evidence and exhibits, because I believe that he didn't have many of the documents until today, that is to say earlier on. Some documents we don't know the source of, others are statements, articles and so on. I just don't understand. Had I done this in my cross-examination -- before my cross-examination, had I given him a binder as thick as this to use just prior to the examination of the witness, it would not have been in order. We don't know the origins, we don't know the source, we don't know what they are about, and we received this five minutes before the start of proceedings today. Nor did the Prosecution ever present these documents before. They are the Prosecution, Your Honours. They are the ones who have accused the clients so it is up to them, and that was the same case with the previous two binders. Are we going to continuously receive new documents which have never been tendered before? Your Honours, I should at least like to be given time to become acquainted with the contents of these many documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott. First of all, I want to know whether the Chamber has been provided with those binders of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm told that you have been, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To respond very briefly, Mr. President, Your Honours, well, I see we are back -- I see we are back to the old situation. Your Honours, during the Prosecution case, we were never provided any documents prior to cross-examination. The Prosecution has, as a courtesy -- and I don't think there is any requirement -- the only thing the Chamber had required of us before was to provide a list at some point. That's the only ruling this Chamber has made in that respect. And we have done much more than that. After -- as a result of a tremendous effort on our part, we have amassed and put together, to assist the Chamber and the Defence and the witness, the documents -- many of the documents or most of the documents that would be used during cross-examination. Indeed, it may be that we will not, in fact, use all of these given time constraints, but nonetheless, that is a binder. Not only have we not -- in our respectful submission, Your Honour, not done anything wrong, we have gone over and above what's required of us to facilitate these proceedings. And finally the only other comment I would make is that, in fact, many of these exhibits have been previously admitted and simply -- but are nonetheless very relevant to the examination of this witness and are not new materials. But even if they are, even if some materials are new, Your Honour, we submit this is entirely appropriate for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, frankly speaking, I'm very sympathise with you because maybe we are from the same legal system in which that all the documents should be disclosed before the trial. The other day, this Trial Chamber made an order asking for the list of the documents be provided before the cross-examination. We believe that we made this ruling during the Prosecution's case in chief with the sole purpose to facilitate the proceedings of the trial. There is no substantial change of the jurisprudence before this Tribunal. We are very glad that the Prosecution provided us with this binder of documents so that we could know what he will be talking about during his cross-examination. Mr. Krsnik, this is his cross-examination, not direct examination, which is entirely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am absolutely and fully conscious that this is cross-examination. But Your Honours, I remember when I was in the position of doing the cross-examination what I had to do vis-a-vis the Prosecution, what I was supposed to do. And that was quite recently. There is your ruling, your decision, when I had to provide written documents and furnish them to the Prosecution, the documents that I was going to use in my own cross-examination. I had to inform them on time. And this is the same procedure. But in this case, the Prosecution, in my opinion, is privileged. Plus, Your Honour, I see that some of these documents are taken from the famous Zagreb archives. Do they mean to tell us that they came by those documents only yesterday? And it is the position of the Defence -- my position and the position of the Defence in its cross-examination was not the same. That is my own personal view and my line of thinking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you have to bear in mind that we made that ruling during the direct examination from the Prosecution. So it applies to both parties. As I have already said, that the purpose for providing us with the list of documents is solely to facilitate the proceedings of the trial. There's no substantial changes of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. So no matter you or we like it or not, we have to live with it because that's the cross-examination, not the direct examination. In a direct examination, you have the obligation to provide all those documents beforehand but not in the cross-examination. I have already said that I quite sympathise with you because maybe we are from the same legal system. But there are some people in this trial, including your co-counsel, Mr. Meek, who is much more familiar than us with this kind of procedure. Yes, Mr. Scott, could you tell us how long you're going to take for your cross-examination. Well, I understand that you mentioned several times during the direct examination by the Defence counsel about the principle of the tu quoque.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, my goal -- and obviously I have not timed this by any means. But my goal is to take significantly less time than the direct examination, which by our measure was approximately 6 hours and 40 minutes. Having said that, I fully expect that at least part of the cross-examination will take us into tomorrow, which should be -- even by tomorrow morning would be only about half of the time that the Defence took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we received a written filing by the accused, notice for additional time for direct examination. They asked for five hours. But because in the very exceptional situation, they lasted a little bit longer, as you calculated, 6 hours and 40 minutes. So the wrongdoings of the other side is not a good excuse for you to have the same period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course not. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm not going to limit your time. I'll just try to advise you that you have to do your cross-examination as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, shall we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Today we will have the cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May it please the Court. Cross-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to comment, sir, that because of the configuration of the courtroom, I'm not always going to be looking directly at you or it may seem that my questions are not being directed to you in a face-to-face way, but unfortunately, because of the way the courtroom is laid out, it's difficult to do that and also use the microphone. So it's not any discourtesy to you if I don't always turn towards you, please. Sir, from the first to the last, from March 1992 to November 1993, you were a senior army in the -- senior officer in the army of the Republic of Croatia, sent by Franjo Tudjman, the HDZ political party and the Croatian government to do their bidding in Herceg-Bosna in support of the goal of a greater Croatia. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is completely untrue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please provide the witness with a copy, in particular, the B/C/S version of PT-7?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, there are about six particular statements of facts which could be separate questions in that statement. I mean, is this witness denying every single bit of it: That he was a senior officer in the army of the Republic of Croatia; two, that he was sent by Franjo Tudjman; three, that it was also associated with the HDZ political party; four, the Croatian government -- it is a very complex statement. Does Mr. Praljak disagree with every aspect of it or some of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark, in the course of today and perhaps tomorrow, we will probably go through all -- each of those items in some detail, and simply, with the Court's leave, as an introductory question, I put the overall proposition to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like for to you please look at what's been admitted into evidence as Exhibit PT-7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for the record -- and perhaps the usher could assist us by putting, if you have it, the English version on the ELMO. This is a transcript of a meeting in the offices of the President of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, on the 8th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik? I'm sorry, I could not see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a technical comment. May we give Mr. Praljak enough time to look through the document? Because he's seeing it for the first time and he didn't have it to read over last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's a reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the -- Mr. President, the entire document -- I only intend to take the witness to a small number of excerpts. The entire document is approximately this long. So if you would like to have him read it, I suppose we could have a recess and come back and proceed with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may direct the witness to a particular page or paragraph which concerns with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to direct your attention to the first page of the B/C/S version. It should be the first page that's in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could ask the usher to please put on the overhead or the ELMO the first page in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to orient you, sir, and the Court, I'm going to direct your attention to the first part. This is a meeting held by President Tudjman with members of -- representatives of the Central Bosnia HVO and Mr. Tudjman -- President Tudjman starts out by saying, "Gentlemen, I wish to welcome the representatives of the Central Bosnian municipalities with whom we are having this meeting at their request, in the presence of the President of the HVO of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Boban, a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mirko" -- perhaps it should be Miro -- "Lasic. Minister Susak will also be coming when this meeting is over. We agreed just now that you from the Central Bosnian municipalities should set out your problems. Be brief, be accurate and truthful so that this remains as a document." Now, sir, let me direct your attention, please, to in your version, page 4/2, in the English version to what's been --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to refer, for reference, to the last two digits of the numbers on the upper corners -- upper right corner of the page, and the reason for that is because the translations of some of these documents were done in segments, and in some instances the page numbering starts over again on the bottom. So I will simply refer to -- for instance, I'm going to refer now to page 12, which in the upper right corner in the English version -- the full number, so that the record is clear, would be R0180812. But if the Court -- with the Court's permission, in the future, I'll just refer to that number as page 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you have 4/2, I'll direct your attention to this. And the reason I'm directing your attention is I will put some questions to you about this. This is Zoran Maric speaking. He says, "However, we are working on this since they have seen what the extremist part of their party has done. I would ask, we in Busovaca, or rather in the central part of Central Bosnia, do not have any educated men. While Mr. Praljak was in Travnik, things were moving along fine. But as soon as he left, things changed for the worse and the situation turned for the worse. There is no military discipline. Crime became prevalent and some military commanders have taken over the civilian authority and behave like that. That is why I would ask that Mr. Praljak be returned to help us with this." If I can direct your attention to, in your copy, sir, page 8/3, and in the English version page 47, can you please find this part on the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We could not find the place. Would you please give us more indications?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Again, as I was trying to do, if you look for page 47, using the number in the upper right corner of the page, the last two digits of the transcript of that number, page 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, there is some problem here. Our first case, if you're talking about the draft translation number, is R0181149, and it's called, on the bottom right hand corner, Exhibit PT-7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We don't have a page 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is in -- and again, the numbering, just because of the way it was translated, is a bit -- admittedly a bit confusing. But if you'll leaf further back in the document, not forward but leaf back, you should find a number R0181147. If the usher -- does the usher have that on the ELMO? All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could -- we'd like to know where the meeting was held, on what date, how, when, et cetera. Could the Prosecution inform us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. It's on the first page of the transcript. This was a meeting. At the first page, a meeting of the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman with the representatives of Central Bosnian municipality and of the HVO of Herceg-Bosna with their associates, held on the 8th of March, 1993, beginning at 11.15 hours. Presiding, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, President of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention, sir, to page -- what we're calling 47. Perhaps in the future we'll try to work out some better paging system. Direct your attention to this part on that page, and in your version 8/3. President Tudjman says -- for the English readers, it's toward the bottom half of the page: "Therefore the HDZ -- if it been for the HDZ, the firmness which has rallied the majority of the Croatian people, we would not have been able to pursue this policy. We would not have Croatia. Of course, the issue of the Croatian people who remain outside our provinces is a very delicate one. But once we get to -- once this agreement is reached, then we shall see, and then we will have to be on the basis of reciprocity and security for those people guarantees there, or in some areas there may be voluntary relocations. The HDZ is safeguarding, in other words, as the political force which enabled us to pursue this policy." Top of the next page, or continuing your version, sir: "We will get Praljak back and see who else we can get back of the Bosnian-Herzegovinan people." I believe there's one last reference. If I can ask the Chamber to go to page 28. It's towards the end of the document again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, but I haven't got the transcript in front of me and I have understood that Mr. Praljak was not at the meeting at all and now he is asked for his comments and to speculate. That's my first point. And second, you can't extract from the overall context a portion of a text. Could the witness be informed about the entirety of the text he's being questioned about. They're asking him to speculate, point A. And second, only certain portions are read out to him out of context. I think it would be fair to inform the witness of the whole document, as he's being asked to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In my understanding, there's no question to this moment. We are still waiting for the question from the Prosecution. Then we'll make the decisions on this respect. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to page 9/4 of the B/C/S version, again page 28 of the English version. And this is the last excerpt that I will direct you to for these purposes before my questions. And this is -- this is the Minister of Defence, Gojko Susak speaking, speaking on -- towards the top page 28. "Your meeting today is going to be useful to you in that you can go back to your place and say over there in Busovaca, Novi Travnik, or Vitez that you were with the president of the state - this is his view - and they will trust you more than if you were to say you were interpreting something or trying to explain who was the one supporting you. That is the essence of today's meeting with the president. You will do everything else with Mate or Mate will work with us. There is not much beating about the bush here." And then Susak continues: "Two things. Praljak warned me about what you've just mentioned, that there is no commander. We did not withdraw Praljak. Praljak has to go -- had to go to a seminar in the Netherlands that had been agreed six months before. He is coming back Wednesday evening, and he's going back there on Thursday morning. Praljak is permanent down there. Praljak was not withdrawn but came here for a purpose. He had a military seminar in the Netherlands which we have to be present at, and he was the one proposed to attend it six months ago. We will send Praljak -- we will send - excuse me - Praljak has made a list of names of several colonels and majors including the young Luburic to send down there. The work of the party." Now, sir, going back to the opening question that I put to you, is it not true, sir - I ask you again - that you were sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina both in 1992 and continuously in 1993 by President Franjo Tudjman and you knew and others knew that you were acting at the direction of the Croatian state? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although the Prosecutor asked several questions framed in one, to make my answers more precise I have to split them into several questions so as to be able to answer. Before this Honourable Court, I never denied that prior to going to Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was an officer -- a high ranking officer in the army of the Republic of Croatia. I did not deny that other people in the army of the Republic of Croatia, including the young Mr. Luburic, who's mentioned here, went to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because they had been born there, because they had lived there, because that is where their families were, to fight against the Serb attack, which was clear, obvious, and ruthless. I am not aware of this meeting. I was not present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me interrupt you, sir. My apology. But I'm not suggesting and nor should you understand that I'm suggesting that you were at the meeting. My question to you, however, is: This meeting reflects what in fact was true, doesn't it? You had been sent by Tudjman to Bosnia before and you were being sent back by him again; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, here we have President Tudjman's transcript. And you know that the Defence has been challenging the authenticity of this document. Now, the Prosecution refers to it as if it were authentic and authenticated and as if what was said at this meeting is true, and on top of it all invites the witness to comment on this. I do not think that cross-examination can be conducted in this way. And before that, a witness needs to be warned that this is a transcript of the president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, that this was done in his office, that this transcript was obtained in this and that way and -- because the witness must be told which documents are being used and read from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think the question is the Prosecutor asked the witness whether he had been sent by Mr. Tudjman to Bosnia before and whether he was being sent back by him again. That's a -- that's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is right. But then why read this transcript, which the Defence challenges and says they are counterfeit? Why -- why didn't he then ask him: Did President Tudjman send you to Bosnia? Why then read from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, because from this transcript, the Prosecution have some doubts about that. So he wants to ask a question to this person whether he was sent by Mr. Tudjman or not. That's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, the Defence has a different view, but we shall abide by your decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you may answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first part of the answer is very clear, but I think it goes beyond this. I was not sent down there. I placed myself at the disposal of my own free will. And I was always so ready to go down there. And even in this document, which has not been verified, even this document showed that I was always ready to help with the good, not with the bad. So for instance, such officer -- officers of international forces were also down there. Sir, under the international auspices of all the members of the United Nations, for instance, there wouldn't have been this massacre in Srebrenica had everybody gone there. And I wasn't there -- I wasn't sent there. And from all this that we see, we do not read that I was issued an order to go down there. But people are asking for -- to go down there to do good. And it was for moral, for ethical reasons, not to try to restrain evil and suffering. That is why I went down there. And I'm not denying this. But not under the order of either President Tudjman or the Minister of War, Susak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that you were playing semantics with the word "order." You went down there at the direction of your president, your president, to serve the wishes of him and his government. And that's the truth of it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has answered this question. And these are -- my apologies. I merely wanted to hear what Mr. Meek had to tell me. The witness has answered this question in full, and this now is turning into a -- into an argument, into a discussion. This is what the Prosecution is doing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe the witness is going to answer this question. Let us hear him again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is the nuances which determine the heart of the whole matter. Sir, would you from dozens of meetings that President Tudjman held with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- also try to draw conclusions --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... any question has nothing to do with Mr. Izetbegovic. My question was very simple. You went to Bosnia not only once but on a number of occasions at the behest of President Tudjman and the Croatian government, did you not, sir? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you use the word "nuance" as the gist of the problem that you are talking about, then with no interruptions will you be able to obtain from me the answer that will suit you. And sir, I will go back to the gist of your question, and that was I did not go there on the basis following an order. I went there of my own free will. And I never used an interpretation with nuances. I will answer as is proper for the sake of the truth and not to please you. I'm very sorry, but that's how it will be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can assure you, sir, that I'm not here to ask you to give answers that please me but to tell the Chamber the truth. And that's the only purpose for your being here. Sir, you've been very critical of the Muslims in various respects. You have -- you and others have complained that the Muslims were slow to react to the Serb aggression and in fact that they were passive. Is that your position as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by the words that you used, "very critical"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's plain English, and I hope the translation is adequate for you. You have complained about -- you -- you and others have complained about that the Muslims were too slow and too passive in reacting to the Serb aggression. And you know full well what I'm talking about sir. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, others. I do not know who they are, so let us exclude that. I will speak in my own name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not rather critical. I was critical as much as it corresponded to the truth, a rational judgement, a rational assessment and facts. Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you were critical of the Muslims for being too passive towards the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is critical insofar as the truth as facts necessitated it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're telling this Chamber, sir, is that in fact the Croats were more proactive militarily and in fact that the Croats were more aggressive militarily than the Muslims were. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of your question, I already answered that one in this Court once, because the Croat people, before the war, in the Republic of Croatia, had already experienced all the forms and crimes of the Serb aggression. It was more ready, not more aggressive but more ready, better prepared, for the defence. This defence started with stopping tanks and singing around those tanks in -- when they set off towards Polog. The standing ovation to President Alija Izetbegovic when he came to see that the tanks of the Yugoslav People's Army be let through from Polog to Kupres, and that was the answer and clear evidence that there was no hate, that the Croat people felt no hatred towards Mr. Alija Izetbegovic or the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question, and I can tell you and the Chamber we will indeed be here a long time if you do not answer my questions. The question is this: The Croats, then -- you're saying the Croats were more proactive militarily than the Muslims were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to this interpretation of the witness's answer by the Prosecution, because if the Prosecution asks complex questions, conditional questions, then the witness must be allowed to answer them in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness went into the answer about Izetbegovic and at the end talking about there was no hate -- that the Croat people felt no hatred towards Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. That has absolutely nothing to do with the question I put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yeah, I agree with you, but I believe that this witness has answered your question already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If that's the case, Mr. President, I will move on, if the Chamber understands that and is satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992, is it not the case that there were a high percentage of Muslims in HVO units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Mostar and around Mostar, where I was, the percentage of the HVO units -- the percentage of Muslims in the HVO units was rather high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, sir, weren't the Muslims less nationalistic in joining the HVO in very substantial numbers and fighting against the Serbs with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind as to explain to me the meaning of the word "nationalism"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, sir, I won't. I think you understand that word well. If there is a Muslim unit -- a Muslim HVO -- excuse me, an HVO unit that was 50 per cent Muslim, let's say - and you said that many had a high percentage of Muslims - and if that unit participated in liberating, for example, Mostar, from the Serbs, then you would agree, wouldn't you, that the Muslims then are at least 50 per cent responsible for liberating Mostar, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm also afraid that this examination will last for a very long time if the Prosecutor continues this way. This question -- and I was objected to by the Prosecution that this witness was not an expert and that he had not come here to testify as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think your objection is well directed, Mr. Krsnik. At this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the witness is asked to speculate, to make some hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I agree on this point. Well, Mr. Scott, you could not ask this kind of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll ask it differently, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said a moment ago that in the HVO units around Mostar - and I'm looking at line 23 - that there was a high percentage -- excuse me, it's higher up. It's in line 14 on page 19: That there was a high percentage of Muslims in HVO units, it was rather high. Now, whatever that percentage was, sir, whether it was 20 per cent, 35 per cent, 50 per cent, 60 per cent, to the extent that was true, the Muslims played, to that extent, just as much a part in liberating Mostar, as an example, than the Croats did, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while ago, the Prosecutor said that assuming that they constituted 50 per cent, that then -- that then they would have played a 50 per cent role in the liberation of Mostar. In the second question, he completely changes the drift of his first question and says, "If they participated, then they played as much a part in liberating to the extent to which they participated in the HVO." And my answer to that is correct. Yes. They should be paid their due for the liberation of Mostar in so far -- to the extent to which they participated in the liberation of Mostar, and that is not more than 35 men. And it is precisely because unfortunately because -- unfortunately they were less ready psychologically and therefore less prepared militarily for it because their leadership kept telling them that it would not be their war, and that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be avoided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, you're going back -- you're confirming your earlier answer that the Croats, rather than the Muslims, were more proactive militarily and more aggressive than the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, how can you join equality -- how can you put together proactivity and aggressiveness? What do you mean by the word "aggressiveness"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we will move on. We do not accept your number of 35 men but we will move on with that. You've also said - and you are were shown a series of exhibits - that the Croatian government gave approvals and facilitated the movement of arms and supplies to the Bosnian Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia enabled the supply of foodstuffs and weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm going to ask for an example -- I'm not going to take -- we don't have the time to go through every one of these exhibits again, but I'll ask the usher to please put before you Exhibit D1/51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Krsnik, are you going to furnish us with a list of the documents you used? Because we got a little bit confused with all those documents. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I indicated earlier or yesterday, because we start trial at 9.00 a.m., the Registry does not open until 9.30. I have these. They will be filed at the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But I have to remind you that you had the whole afternoon yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and we had much work to do and we completed it last night, and we will file it at the first break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've said a moment ago, sir, that Croatia enabled the supply. Sir, can you tell the Chamber who was Ivan Cermak who approved the particular shipment that is reflected or transfer that's reflected on page -- excuse me, D1/51?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan Cermak was Assistant Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, responsible for logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why would he have to be involved -- just explain. Not being critical. Just explain why would he have to be involved in approving a shipment of arms or ammunition to the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Croatian army, together with Muslims, in Zagreb was working towards -- that all the -- to transport all the things that were being collected, from clothing, all sorts of wear, and weapons, that they be transported through Croatia, which was in the state of war, in a safe manner, and as these convoys have to make very many detours and follow very difficult routes because of the attacks on Sibenik and Zadar, then in order to ensure their safety, the army was the most desirable segment of the Croatian state for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in terms of your direct testimony, are you telling the Chamber that it's your testimony that the Croatian government, throughout the period of the war, had -- including through 1993 and into 1995, that the Croatian government was consistently and freely allowing the passage of arms and supplies to the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Court's leave, I would like to give a more extensive answer. Namely, in spite of the embargo on the delivery of weapons, certain international forces and powers allowed a certain form of violation of that embargo, and the military aid was received from some countries by -- and it arrived by air to Rijeka and Zagreb airports. A part of this aid was intended for Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Throughout the war, the assistance to Muslims never stopped, either humanitarian or military, although -- although at times it was very difficult to achieve, and I do not deny that there were certain problems. The Honourable Court saw yesterday how, for instance, when I had to climb the APC of the United Nations in Citluk, and contrary to the will of the people, how I had to break through -- pave the way for the humanitarian convoy intended for Muslims in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the answer has gone on for some 10 or 15 lines and we are far away from my question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question to you was rather simple. Is it your position -- you're telling the Chamber that throughout the fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including 1993 and thereafter, that the Croatian government was consistently allowing the free flow of arms and ammunition to the Bosnian Muslims? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by the word "consistently"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could the usher please hand the witness Exhibit D1/68?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that -- a map that was used in your direct examination yesterday. And I want to direct your attention -- and I can't point -- really point to it very well in a way that will show you, but if you find Zenica, which is approximately in the middle of the map, and you look immediately above Zenica, there are two blue areas. Do you see that? Do you see those areas?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also then somewhat to the right, quite a way -- a bit -- well, whatever, to the right of those two, there is another blue area around, I believe, Tuzla. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you've talked about the shipments, in connection with, in particular, the ones we were shown yesterday, Exhibits D1/51 through about 64 -- /64, do you have any information -- can you assist the Chamber in any way by telling them what the destination of those shipments were? Do you know that, in fact, they were not going to either those two blue areas or to the blue area around Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain this yesterday, but the map is self-explanatory. There is only one and only way in which the complete armament could get into this territory, and that is the Republic of Croatia Herzegovina onward. And if the convoy went past Mostar or next to Rama by Prozor, then its further fate was determined by the Muslim forces which received that convoy. Bihac -- Croatia shipped whatever was necessary to Bihac by air, and after the conflict broke out, in the Lasva Valley, we sent -- we used helicopters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... isn't it true, number 1, you don't know -- you cannot verify that one single of those items, one bullet, in fact, got to Muslim military force, can you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear what the question means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no personal knowledge that you can share with this Chamber that a single one of the items reflected in these many letters, rocket-propelled grenades, RPGs, 82-millimetre rounds, 107-millimetre rounds. You have no personal information to provide this Chamber that a single one of those items in fact reached the Muslim armed forces, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that reached the Muslim armed forces because I personally many times was there when the convoy was let through. And in 1992 in the spring of that year, I personally armed the Muslims, organised the training of Muslim units --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And later --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did you personally -- just to follow up on your answer just now, did you personally observe and participate the transfer of weapons to Muslim armed forces in 1993, personally?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once again, the question arises: Transport, participate, supervise. Now, did I know? Was I personally there in some of the transports? Sir, your questions are so generalised that whichever answer I give, it won't be an entirely accurate one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the answer I put -- the question I put to you - excuse me - was quite direct. You answered a previous question by verifying when I asked you for personal information that you were personally present and involved in some of these transfers. I'm simply following up on your own answer. And you said this happened in 1992. And in the words of your own previous answer, did you so participate personally any time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did participate in the course of 1993 in letting pass certain transports of food and arms. And you saw one of those convoys yesterday on the film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying that convoy that we saw yesterday was not only humanitarian aid. You're telling this Chamber that that was also a shipment of arms.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That particular convoy did not consist of weapons. I precisely stated that that convoy was carrying humanitarian aid alone. But I did say that on several occasions when we examined the humanitarian convoys, we uncovered a certain quantity of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll come back to that in a minute, sir. Isn't it true -- and the reason I -- one of the reasons I showed you this map -- isn't it true that there were certain areas that despite the conflict around Busovaca and Vitez and despite the conflict around Mostar and that region between the Muslims and Croats, that there were other parts, including the area around Tuzla, where the Croats and the Muslims fought together against Serbs throughout the war. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true -- partially true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any information, sir, that the armed shipments, for instance, that you're talking about did not -- were not going to those areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina where throughout the war the Muslims and Croats were fighting together against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a HVO brigade in Tuzla which the Muslims had disbanded at the beginning of the conflict between the Croats and Muslims. It is correct that humanitarian and military aid went to those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to go back to your question about the smuggling of weapons as part of humanitarian aid convoys. Help me with this, sir: If it is your position before this Chamber, as you said yesterday and confirmed again this morning, that the state of Croatia openly and fully facilitated the shipment of arms to the Bosnian Muslims, why would anyone have to smuggle them in humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was always a lack of weapons of that kind. The states of the former Yugoslavia were under an embargo, and the Republic of Croatia under those circumstances and conditions was not even able to procure sufficient quantities of weapons for itself either. So the procurement of weapons was something that everybody engaged in, the Croats and Muslims alike, outside the country by collecting funds for the purchase of weapons throughout Europe and the world on the black market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask you about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then they had to smuggle them in every possible way, not only through Europe but through Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you've told this Chamber that the -- there was a free flow of weapons and supplies -- and you've suggested -- I put it to you -- you've suggested to these Judges -- you're trying to tell these Judges that Croatia freely supported the Muslims in Bosnia throughout the war and were sending arms and shipments and supplies. And I'm putting it to you, sir, that's simply not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that's your problem. I claim the following -- and I can put it in a nutshell in one sentence: Never in the history of warfare has one country and one nation, one peoples, assisted another nation so much by training it, by receiving it, by arming it, in order to prepare it and raise it to the level of the ability to attack part of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was so much assistance, as you just said, that in fact you searched -- you had to search humanitarian convoys to make sure that no weapons were getting to the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, Mr. Prosecutor, at the same time they were in a very difficult position. Croatia wanted, and the Croatian people wanted, to preserve the remains of what remained after the Serbs, what the Serbs had not taken. Simultaneously it was very difficult to know that the arms that were let through would be used against the Serbs, would be used against those who were supplying those weapons, which were the Croats, the Croats that were either supplying them or letting them pass. So it was a duality. The situation was very precarious. We let convoys pass, but we had this dilemma: What was ethical, what was moral, and what was militarily advantageous in a situation of that kind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last document you've given us in the Defence case on this is dated the 30th of March, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document? Could you tell me please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe it is, sir -- it's D1/64.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness can't find his way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I can find my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant, Witness, was that the witness can't find the document and hasn't got the number D1, et cetera. So I think that we ought to say which document we mean and quote its number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe I just did, Mr. President. If the usher could assist us, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just confirm for me, sir, that the date of that document is the 30th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the date is the 30th of March, 1993. That's what it says on the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we're a couple of minutes earlier than the usual break time, but I'm about to switch to another topic. And with the Court's leave, this might be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Bring in the witness, Mr. Usher. Yes, Mr. Scott. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as of the end of July, 1993, you were the senior HVO military commander, that is over the entire HVO military apparatus; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't senior. I was an HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who above you, sir, in terms of an HVO officer, who was above you in the chain of command, if it wasn't you, if you weren't the top?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terms, I was at the top, and above me was Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you telling this Chamber then that you reported directly to Mate Boban as your superior?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, isn't it true that in the capacity of the senior HVO officer, you presided over the mass arrest and expulsion of Muslims from the Stolac municipality in July and August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in command, nor did I preside over or implement the arrest of Muslims that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the 28th of July, 1993, you issued an order -- you issued an order to all HVO units in the southeast Hercegovinian operative zone to raise combat readiness to the top level and take up positions in their area of responsibility, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we see the order and allow the witness to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have time to give -- I can put facts to the witness, respectfully, I submit. I can put facts to the witness. He can either agree or disagree. If we have to go every single document, this binder will be about four times as fat and we will be here for some weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, shall we ask the witness whether he issued this order or not first? And later on, if there is need for that purpose, you have to show that order to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was exactly the question I put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, you issued an order on the 28th of July, 1993, to raise the combat readiness of the entire HVO southeast Herzegovina operative zone to mobilise them for a campaign?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that we are dealing here with very serious accusations, and that I am testifying to the truth and wish to testify to the truth, I am personally ready to remain here several weeks, if that is what is needed. I would like to see my order. Would you show me my order, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the time, Mr. Praljak, that of course is entirely up to the Chamber and I cannot give you an answer to that. Sir, isn't it correct that the action started on approximately the 1st of August, 1993? On the 1st of August, four mosques in Stolac were destroyed and during the following night, the night between the 1st and 2nd of August, 1993, HVO trucks went around the town of Stolac, picked up all the Muslim women, children and old people and took them away?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what way, Mr. Prosecutor, do you think I can know those facts from here? I would like to have a map to show you all the problems that existed in commanding over such a large territory and specify dates, because during those times, I was at many places, so I do not have the facts at my disposal which you are referring to. The order of combat readiness --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the date, sir, are between approximately the 1st -- well, the mobilisation was on the 28th of July, and the action continued until approximately the 5th or so of August. And sir, the reason I asked you about this and the reason I expect you to know this, if you do, is because you were the commander of these forces. And you've told this Chamber in great detail yesterday and in the direct examination, could speak in great detail about events and actions. I'm asking you to speak in such equal detail on cross-examination. So I put it to you again, sir, that what I said to you is true, isn't it? On the 1st of August, 1993, four mosques were destroyed in Stolac and Muslim women, children, and elderly were collected and put on trucks; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are not conducting an investigation. This is a cross-examination. I don't recall the Prosecution providing any witness to testify to the destruction of the mosque or the expulsion from Stolac. That's the first point. The second point is that we have here a witness, who as far as I understand is at the disposal. And he said himself that he is ready to testify as long as is necessary. I consider that it is necessary to clarify matters. And if the Prosecutor is bringing up issues of this kind, let him produce the orders, because he has not produced witnesses to testify to that and I don't know where he gets his facts from. May I -- I would like to see an order dated such and such where so and so happened, so many women were taken off. And if that happened, then I'm sure the Prosecutor has the document to show the witness and the witness will then be able to comment on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe that this question is very simple. The Prosecution is just asking the knowledge of this witness, whether he knows or not about this operation. And if he knows, what kind of a role he played during that incident. That's a very simple question. Let us hear this question. If the witness said -- if the witness -- sorry, if the witness said he does not know at all about this incident, so it's over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, if we proceed in that way. But that was not how I understood the Prosecutor to accept answers. I agree precisely with what you just said, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, sometimes your question, I must say, is up to the point, but it's very complicated. You know, because of the translation and because of different cultural background, there will be different interpretations of your question. So would you please split your question into small pieces and ask one question after another so that to come across a very clear message to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, it's true, is it not, is that on the 1st of August, 1993, the HVO destroyed four mosques in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that on the 1st of August, 1993, the HVO collected the Muslim women, children, and elderly in Stolac, put them on trucks, and took them away?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, 1993, approximately 2.000 Muslim civilians were taken -- collected in Stolac and taken to Blagaj through Buna, on buses and trucks. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the witness -- if the witness has the binder -- can be given the binder of exhibits, please. And I will direct everyone in the courtroom to Exhibit 559.2. And I will tell everyone that -- I hope this may be a rare occasion. It is not the first. It is the last exhibit in the binder because of some changes that were made this morning. But it is the last exhibit in the binder, Mr. President, 559.2. And in particular, if the witness could be shown the B/C/S version of that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Miljenko Obradovic was one of your commanders, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obradovic, yes. But I don't think his first name was Miljenko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, a brigade -- a battalion commander -- if you were the chief and the senior HVO officer for all of Herceg-Bosna, which you said you were, then this battalion commander fell under your chain of command and responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the battalion is a subordinate to the brigade commander, and the brigade commander is subordinate to the commander of the operative zone, and the commander of the operative zone is subordinate to myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that on the 4th of August, 1993, one of your subordinate officers, as part of the campaign which you yourself mobilised on the 28th of July, 1993 issued this order, in part: Number one, round up the Muslim population in the wider territory in the depth of the area of responsibility of the 3rd Battalion. Two, when rounding them up, do not pay attention to age. Three, gather detained persons in two collection centres. Four, on completion of the task, report to superior command. Five, in case of resistance by them, respond by opening fire from personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all three of us here are controlling the indictment, looking at the indictment, and want to see where this is stated, where the Prosecutor is making these charges. This is not an investigation. He can't have a cross-examination on something that he has not set out as being a charge in the indictment, although, of course, the witness is ready to answer. But I am objecting because I don't see this in the indictment. Nor did the Prosecution present witnesses. And now he is asking the witness to state his views on something he doesn't know about, so perhaps he's opening an investigation. He could have done that seven years ago, and he's waiting for the Defence to bring witnesses forward in order to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a further objection, Mr. President. And that is that the question asked by my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, is such a long one, complicated and involved, that it is debatable whether the witness is able to give a yes or no answer to the question as it has been posed by the Prosecutor and as the Prosecutor requires. Because a complex question requires a complex answer. So my question -- my objection is this, and I should like to ask the Prosecutor to ask simple questions and questions that are easy to understand and that will put us back on track, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President. I can't -- number 1, I'll save that for another time. I can't think of anything, respectfully to the Chamber, that could be more important than the credibility of this witness. And if this witness -- and I represent to the Chamber I have very good foundations for asking these questions and I will take this witness to some additional documents momentarily. But nothing could be possibly more relevant to this Chamber in assessing the evidence of this witness than his credibility, and this goes directly to the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we agree with the objections issued -- raised by Mr. Seric. It is a complicated question. We do not agree with the objections raised from Mr. Krsnik. In this aspect, I think the Prosecution is entitled to test the credibility of this witness. Mr. Scott, could you please put your question another way?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've asked to see an order, and I've shown you an order, 559.2, which I put to you is one of your subordinate officers', and simply ask: That's the order; that's what it says; doesn't it? And that is, in fact, what happened in the Stolac area in early August, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: I was the commander of the army. Let me repeat: That army had a defence line stretching 2.000 kilometres. Let me repeat: It is possible that I issued an order to raise the combat readiness in a certain locality because that is part of the daily orders issued by every army commander. But I don't see the connection between my possible order on raising combat readiness and the order -- an order signed by the commander of a battalion, of one brigade, of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling this Chamber that the President of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, knew more about what was going on on the confrontation line in Bosnia, knew more about the details and what had happened there during these days, than you did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. I object to that question. It is more than obvious that this is purely speculation which is contained in the question and in a possible answer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is no speculation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, it's not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no speculation whatsoever. I ask the witness to be shown Exhibit PT-10 and you'll see Mr. Tudjman's own words. There is no speculation at all. Can the witness please be shown Exhibit PT-10? For the record, while that's happening, Mr. President, to try to save sometime and to respond to counsel's earlier question, this exhibit, admitted into evidence already, is the record of a meeting in the Office of the President of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, in Zagreb, on the 21st of September, 1993, beginning at 1830 hours, chaired by, on the first page, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, the President of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to direct your attention, please, to what would be in the B/C/S version, 2/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to the Chamber, please, what would be, again using the same system as before, the last two digits of the number appearing in the upper right corner. I would ask the -- ask that this also be put on the ELMO. It's page 74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the witness is reading, Your Honours, we have studied the order signed by Miljenko Obradovic, and this document has been tendered for the first time, and we are just checking but we think that it is in the last two binders that the Trial Chamber rejected. But we are checking to see whether it is incorporated into the last two binders of exhibits that the Trial Chamber refused. We don't know the origins and source of the document, whether it is an authentic document, whether it is a falsified document or not, a forgery. I don't see that it has a stamp or anything else. All that I see is that it says the Zagreb Croatian State Archives. And we know all about those archives. Now, I don't think, Your Honours, that we can allow every document to be introduced which the Prosecutor might see the use of without us knowing its origins and source.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence selects its witnesses. They called this man here to testify, not the Prosecution. When they did that, they made a bundle of much information, highly relevant to this Chamber. Now, I don't know, I don't think this is included in the last two binders of exhibits, but even if it were, we submit, it would make no difference. It's valid to be used for cross-examination to this witness, and it's directly responsive to the allegations that have been put before him. He asked to see an order and we gave him an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. No matter whether it's admitted or not in the Prosecution's case, we have to use these documents because it's a request from the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we know the source of this document, the origin? Can we know that this is not a forgery? How can the Prosecutor claim that it was not planted on him by somebody? The question of the origin of this document -- the Prosecutor can now put thousands of such documents before the witness and then this will turn into what, cross-examination or something else, Your Honours. As far as I know, I was always asked about the origin of a document, whenever I conducted cross-examination, and I always provided an answer to the Court. If this is not a tactic -- if this is not tactical behaviour of the Prosecutor, but the Prosecutor's Office needs to prove something. They are not in the same position as the Defence. I claim that this document is a forgery, that it's false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Scott could shed some light on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this. This is not a proper way to proceed. In fact, counsel tendered many documents during cross-examination, not with any prior witness, if -- having authenticated any of them, providing no foundation. In cross-examination, documents are tendered to a witness for purposes of cross-examination. Now, to understand what Mr. Krsnik -- to take what Mr. Krsnik is saying to heart, what we would have to do is before we could proceed with cross-examination, I would then have to call a series of additional witnesses to authenticate the documents that I would then put to this witness. Now, that is not the procedure in any system I'm aware of. Plus, number 2, this is as it plainly says, the document from the HVO archive. It bears the stamp in the upper right corner. The Chamber has heard witness testimony on a number of occasions, from Mr. Prelec and others, about those identification marks and the documents collected and the process of collecting the documents from the Zagreb archive. It is blatantly clear on the face of the document and the testimony that the Prosecution has already tendered in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: One minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I respected witnesses that the Prosecutor authenticated and to have this document authenticated, we need Mr. Miljenko Obradovic. He's the only one that can do it, and I'm afraid this man does not exist. So the Defence needs to conduct additional investigation and the defence needs to be allowed to do that, and I believe the Prosecutor has closed his case and he may not seek for additional witnesses, because if he does so, then the defence needs to be allowed to conduct further investigation. We promise to bring in the author of every single order. And the Prosecutor, I do not think, has ever produced any single author of any single order. He uses his investigators who are part of the Prosecutor's team and are sitting now in the gallery and watching what is going on here because they obviously are very interested in this. Through third persons, they are trying to prove the authenticity of documents. And going further than that, they're trying to use them in the cross-examination as authentic documents. But the Defence puts it to the Court that this document is false and that it may not be used in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear what the witness is going to tell us. Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I've directed you to page 2/1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's hear the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In answer to what question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this witness asked for the floor to tell us about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the document. Your Honours, I've read the document, and I can explain why I think that this document is not authentic. To begin with, I have never heard of Miljenko Obradovic. There was a brigade commander called Nedeljko Obradovic. And the second important point is the following: The name of the place mentioned in two places Sevac Polje. That is what it says, Sevas Polje, in the third and first part -- or rather, the first item of the order. But the name of that place is Sevas, with an "S" in the end. So that it is very difficult to imagine that somebody coming from the area could twice misspell the name from which that person comes. There is no Sevac Polje. That is Sevas Polje. These are the first and the third items of the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, perhaps the person didn't come from the area. Perhaps this person came from some place in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Obradovics comes from the Stolac area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution, you may proceed with Exhibit PT/10.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to bring you to 2/1; and again for those having the English version, page 74. Sir, I'm going to put this to you, and then I'll have some follow-up questions. Didn't President Tudjman say at this time: "Stolac, I know the importance of Stolac, both as the president of Croatia and, if you will, as a soldier. I know that Stolac and the entire former Jablanica, Kotar were included in the Croatian Banovina in 1989. These are arguments I have upheld since the first day. However, they say that Stolac was predominantly Muslim, and therefore ethnic cleansing has taken place and the Muslims should have been -- what else did he say? Should have" -- and then he changes to Posavina. "Clearly we again tried and did everything in the attempt to preserve the solution from 1939, Derventa, Gradacac, et cetera. You know that we used the Croatian army to the then Bosanska Posavina for a long time."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will stop there to indicate that is a separate area bordering on Croatia in the north-east part of Bosnia, the Posavina, as opposed to the Banovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention next, sir, to page 3/1, or page 77 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that can be put again on the ELMO, the bottom half of that page, 77.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: President Tudjman says: "We tried to sign, as you know -- I signed an agreement with the Muslims in the summer of last year -- on 12 July last year in talks with Turkovic when we signed the agreement. We posed a military agreement to Izetbegovic that would allow the legal engagement of the army. He did not accept it. As far as engagement was concerned, especially there, in the Posavina area, we were fettered from that point of view. Since we did not have a military agreement, we are in a delicate position with our Croatian soldiers. We were at war and we must not say we are at war; however, we are sending them there. The people would not have it, and they deserted, et cetera. We cannot take them to court because that is the way it is politically."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down when he's reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. My apology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, I believe, sir, if I can direct your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Slow down. Yes, Your Honour. My apology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can next ask you, Witness, to look at 5/2 and 5/3. I'm sorry. Yes, pages 84 and 85, the bottom of page 84. President Tudjman is still speaking. The bottom of page 84: "Therefore, not to bring into question just the Croatian state, we had to agree to it. But go now because I too have told our people please settle these refugees in those areas, Tosavici, Stolac, et cetera, to be Croats." On the top of the next page: "So that Croatian people are present there. Then we will in practice the demarcation, and in the future, it will then be important who is there," et cetera. And finally to page 74 and 75 in B/C/S, and page 17 in the English version. Pero Markovic then responds to President Tudjman: "Mr. President, only two questions. When it comes to the territory south of the Buna down to Stolac and back to Capljina, this is an area of approximately 250 kilometres square. There is not a single Muslim there. Croats live there. And we have brought 3.000 Croats from Kakanj, from Travnik too, and Croats from Konjic. All the houses that are sound are full. Their priests have followed in their steps too. President, wait. I said that the containers too and that too -- Pero Markovic, Mr. President, in Tosavici, we have about 100 cottages." If you want to skip down to the next paragraph: "In the Stolac area too my cousin, Dr. Azaco knows more about it, but we have already filled the Stolac area to capacity.
