Our troops have been holding the unchanged line" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm slowing down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Are holding the unchanged lines for 15 months already, where in view of the security we did not settle them close to the line. And now, 20 kilometres from Stolac, maybe even more, from Blagaj, there is not a single Muslim." Now, sir, this was being discussed in the office of the president of the Republic of the Croatia in September 1993, a few weeks after these events happened on the ground. I come back to you, sir. Your subordinate officers knew about it and your ultimate superior officer, Franjo Tudjman, knew about it. And it's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After your 15-minute speech, I do not know what is true and what isn't, and I do not know what you are setting out to prove. If the Honourable Court allows me, I will analyse this in a manner in which I think it should be analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm in the Chamber's hands, Your Honour. If the Chamber wants us to take the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may. You may explain to us, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the document is true - and I do not know if it is - then we can interpret it. President Tudjman is saying what he thinks was the Banovina. And the Banovina existed in the former Yugoslavia. If Banovina was in Konjic and Jablanica, then why didn't the HVO attack Konjic and Jablanica -- if Mr. President Franjo Tudjman thinks so. The discussion about what was Banovina and what was the strategic point, I really do not see wherein the crime. It is a fact that in the place of Stolac itself, there were more Muslims than Croats, but the vicinity of Stolac and villages around Stolac are mostly populated by Croats. In the next item -- under the next item, we go back to the thesis that I mentioned earlier: The Croatian army could not be ordered to go to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that includes Posavina, the Sava valley. So what it refers to is that there were very many deserters, that is, men who refused to cross into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, into the -- into Posavina, although they were fighting there against Serbs and for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thirdly, mention is made here that thousands of Muslims expelled from that area have arrived there to that territory, and they needed accommodation. Then reference is made to the fact that Alija Izetbegovic refused to sign a military agreement which would allow for a high grade of defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I think that this attacks again corroborates all my earlier theses about the manner in which the war was conducted in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the expulsion of the Croat population from [Realtime transcript read in error "Bosnia-Herzegovina"] Central Bosnia, and participation of the Croatian army which could never get such an order and deserters were not punished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, the reason -- isn't it a fact that the reason deserters couldn't be punished, the people who -- some of the people who had refused to go to Bosnia, is because for those deserters to be prosecuted, Croatia would have to admit in a public forum that it was indeed sending its troops into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, the witness did not say that the Croats were expelled from Bosnia-Herzegovina but from Central Bosnia. Only for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question stands, sir: Isn't that true? One of the problems -- in fact it was the transcript we just read. And they talked about the problem. And Tudjman says: "We can't prosecute the deserters because then we would have to admit that we really are there." Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we are at war, not that we are there. That is, Croatia was fighting a defensive war against Serbia, mostly because the International Community requested that, by setting up the UMPA zones in Croatia and wishing to at the same time -- to guarantee the safety of the people who remained in those zones. Several hundred people were killed in those zones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with the question that I put to you, and I will move on to another topic. The Chamber has the transcript and will be able to find the place where -- I'm looking for it again now. The bottom of page 77 of the English version where President Tudjman talks about "We can't take them to court."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page? What is meant here is Croatia's war and not the war of Croatia against Bosnia-Herzegovina. Croatia never declared war on Serbia, nor did Serbia and Yugoslavia declare war on Croatia. It was a war without the declaration of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's your interpretation of it and you asked for the page number. It's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 3/1, the Chamber has that, and we'll see the context in which that's mentioned. Now, sir, you are a citizen -- are you a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but can the witness read page 3/1? Could he be shown page 3/1 first and then allow the witness to read through it because it is the witness that is testifying and not the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I join my colleague in that objection, the objection made by Mr. Krsnik. And let me add one more reason why the objection is in order. The Prosecutor has just said that the context speaks for itself. It is telling the Trial Chamber something which means he opposes the thesis contained in his question with the witness's answer. I think that the witness should be allowed to see the context and be allowed to comment on it. I think that this sounds complicated but it is indeed, in fact, simple, and just and fair towards this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, from the answer of this witness, I believe that the witness has already read that paragraph. Is that true? If not, you have an opportunity to read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was read before, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you want to read it again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've read the paragraph. I was in Posavina too. I know which units did not want to cross over. I know that an order could not be issued. I also know that we are talking here about a war which Croatia never declared. It did not declare war on Yugoslavia, and that there is no military agreement with Alija Izetbegovic, which the Croatian president, from the start, as far as I know, wanted so as to be able to defend themselves against a common foe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Croatia never declared war on the Bosnian Muslims either, did it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am today a citizen, both of the Republic of Croatia and of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if you're asking about those times, it was all Yugoslavia and we were all citizens of Yugoslavia. And we remained as such for considerable time, until the basic papers were set in order which would testify to one's citizenship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you become a citizen of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in 1992 or 1993, when I succeeded in collecting all my papers together for the newly established state. Before that, I was a citizen of the Socialist Federal Republic of Croatia within the frameworks of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you join the HDZ political party?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the HDZ, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you tell the Chamber, please, did the HDZ leadership in Croatia control the HDZ party also in Bosnia, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political problem of the relationship between the two parties was not something of interest to me, and I don't wish to discuss the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what military training you had received prior to going to Bosnia in approximately, as you told us yesterday or the day before, in March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not military-able for the military service in the Yugoslav People's Army, and after three months of it, I was sent home. In the war in Croatia, near Sisak, I went as a volunteer, as being a professional theatre and film producer and director before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, are you saying --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any military training, although I think that I was a talented commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, and I mean -- I sincerely mean -- I don't question your personal courage at all, for getting on that armoured personnel carrier, for instance, but I do ask you this question. How did someone with no prior military training or experience, who had never before been an officer, become, first of all, the Assistant Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and the most senior military officer in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Court doesn't mind, Their Honours don't mind, let me say that I am sufficiently well-educated and sufficiently well-capacitated in organisational terms. I was a sufficiently sure of the ethics and morals of my actions, and I probably progressed and went up the ranks as Napoleon's soldiers perhaps had done before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as you told us now, your experience, your whole professional life, was primarily in the theatre. That was your prior qualification, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both as an electrical engineer, graduated from the university, and as professor of philosophy, I generally dealt with the problems of society, social problems, communist lack of freedom, closing up, arrests, persecutions, and mutilation of every personal, civic and civilian rights and others. But I have read enough --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir -- go ahead, please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If war is a phenomenon, and especially war in Croatia, because of the difficult inheritance of the regime of 1941 to 1945, that burden, and the difficult state of affairs in a country with a communist system, I, in trying to answer one of the more difficult questions that humanity is faced with, and that is the problem of war, in trying to answer that question, I read enough books and literature on the subject from Clausewitz to literature on World War II, to Zhukov, Kontev, Paton, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yet a few minutes ago, you couldn't tell us what "nationalistic" meant. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. Krsnik, allow me. Let me respond. I have to say to you, Mr. Prosecutor, that I could hold a two-hour lecture on the subject here and now. I know full well what nationalism is, what it means. But there is the content of a word as a concept in linguistics. So for us to use a word, we must know exactly what that word means, what its contents are. Otherwise, you will be speaking about one thing and I will be speaking about another. If you have enough time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you off there. I put it to you, sir, that the reason that you were put in these very senior military positions with a total absence of prior training and qualification was because President Tudjman viewed you as someone who would be loyal to him and would do his bidding. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went to the battlefront voluntarily, and my capabilities and knowledge and skill was checked out, and you can check it out, if you bring qualified professionals to do that, which I think, Mr. Prosecutor, you yourself are not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in -- on approximately the 14th of March, 1992, you were appointed the Assistant Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have the date? I can look it up here, yes. Roughly correct, yes, more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Defence Minister of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Gojko Susak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 25th of April, 1992, the Croatian Army General Bobetko issued an order to you when you were serving in the position in Bosnia, having command of the sector Siroki Brijeg, Citluk, Ljubuski and Capljina. Do you recall that? Let me just put it this way: Do you recall receiving orders from General Bobetko in approximately April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of April, 1992, I became commander of the operative zone -- of the southeast operative zone, and I did not receive orders from General Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nor was I subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at a few documents, please. Can I first ask you to look at the first document in the binder, if you have that, is Exhibit 121.1, just to clarify for the record, because you said, I think, a moment ago that Mr. Susak appointed you, and in fact you were appointed Assistant Minister of Defence by Franjo Tudjman, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't challenge that. Let's say it was Dr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I can ask you then to go to Exhibit 124.1, the next document in the binder? Is that not an order from Janko Bobetko to Major General Slobodan Praljak dated the 25th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is an order by General Bobetko, Janko Bobetko, but I say, with a full responsibility of telling the truth, that General Bobetko did not command me. I was not under his command. The papers he sent, I did not read, and that in that respect, I have explained the specific way in which General Bobetko considered that he was playing the role of commander of the southern front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this indicates that you were a major general. You were a major general in what army at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major General in the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yet you were serving as the command of the sector for Siroki Brijeg, Citluk, Ljubuski and Capljina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean over there in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Yes, I was the commander there. But that rank, if that's what you had in mind, Mr. Prosecutor, was worthless except that my -- the people called me General and addressed me as General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the insignia of commander there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you tell, at some point, when you got a number of orders from Janko Bobetko -- and again, sir, we simply don't have the time, unless the Chamber wishes otherwise, to go through every single piece of paper I could possibly put in front of you. Did you ever contact Janko Bobetko and say, "General, I keep receiving orders from you, but by the way, in so many words, take a hike, because you're not my superior officer"? Did you tell General Bobetko that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions, I did have verbal, if I can put it that way, verbal conflicts with General Bobetko. But you see, I liberated the Capljina barracks, and there is certainly no order from General Bobetko ordering me to do so. I led the liberation of Mostar, and once again there is no order to herald -- to unleash an operation of that kind either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a moment, sir. Now, on approximately the 10th of September, 1992, as reflected by Exhibit P172.1, the next document in the binder - there is a B/C/S version which follows - on the 10th of September, 1992, you were appointed once again by Dr. Franjo Tudjman as members of a Council of People's Defence of the Republic of Croatia. You can see a substantial list - well, I say a substantial list, but a list of 14 people - including Gojko Susak, including Janko Bobetko, including Ivan Cermak, a man you identified earlier today, including yourself, and can you tell us in what capacity you served as a member of the Council of the People's Defence of the Republic of Croatia when you were the commanding officer, as you just told us, in Siroki Brijeg, Capljina, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was the commander of the operative zone - that is exactly what I said - the southeast, until the 10th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you continued being in Bosnia after that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: From the 10th of April; interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would go to Bosnia occasionally. I was the commander for a month or a month and a half, although each time when I went down there - and I went down there whenever I could - without any official, formal signatures, through the force of my own authority, quite certain in the morality of my actions, and I would take over a certain measure of command, and the operation to liberate the right bank of the River Neretva, and later on Mostar, too, and this started --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're telling us, you just said it, that you went down to Bosnia, and you're saying with no rank or position, you simply went there and were accepted as the commander in such a way that you then, in your own words, led the liberation of Mostar, led the liberation of Capljina. Is that what you're telling this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: However much you try to change the meaning of my words, I think that my concentration, which emanates from the facts which are in my head, is so great that you will just be losing your time -- wasting time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am ready, precisely, specifically and exactly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if the Chamber wants to cut me off or correct me, I'm sure they will do so. Can you please answer my question? On what authority did you lead the liberation of Mostar and the liberation of Capljina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm afraid that the Prosecutor -- that is to say, had I behaved the way the Prosecutor is behaving now during my cross-examination, and had I addressed witnesses in this manner, I don't think that -- I think that the Prosecutor would be on his feet all the time. I don't think that this can be done, interrupting, not interrupting. The only people that can interrupt here are Your Honours, and I think that once the witness starts giving an answer, I think that he should be allowed to finish. And that is something that Your Honours always insisted upon. You would always allow the witness to finish his answer or finish explaining the thought he was putting forward. And I think that this principle should be respected now as well. So I should like to ask the Prosecutor from refraining -- behaving that way towards the witness. And another question here, we are dealing -- bringing up the Narodne Novine or People's Gazette, I don't know whether they are in fact the Narodne Novine of the Republic of Croatia, that publication. We see just one page and this is the decision on the nominations for the appointments of members of the Council of People's Defence of the Republic of Croatia. I have no confirmation that this is originally taken from the Official Gazette. The Official Gazette is a publication which publishes laws, enacted by the Sabo or assembly in the Republic of Croatia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, as to the last issue you mentioned, we believe that all we need is judicial notice of the existence of this official document. There is no need to testify on the authenticity of this document. That's the first issue. Mr. Scott, my advice is that you have to be a little more patient. Maybe the answer of this witness will answer your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour. Mr. President, I'm being, I assure the Chamber, 100 per cent sincere in what I'm about to say. The witness can give as long answers as he wants. We can spend the next several weeks taking testimony from this witness. And I'll be happy to do so. I'll stand here every day and go through the documents, and I'll put witnesses -- I'll let him talk as long as he wants, but I'm in the Chamber's hands. So if the witness -- if the witness is not going to give responsive answers, with all respect, then either I have to cut him off, which has been the practice in other cases and the practice before Judge May in the Kordic case and other cases, or, Mr. President, you can cut him off. But I'm in the Chamber's -- completely in the Chamber's hands. And as I say, we can take as long as we need be to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I just want to remind you to show some courtesy to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And you may proceed with your question. I don't think the last question is answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The last question was, I believe .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've said several times that you went down to Bosnia-Herzegovina and you led several very substantial military actions. And yet you've told us, I believe, in the last few minutes you had no rank, position, or formal mandate if you will from anyone. You had no assignment or task either from the government of Croatia or from, what you've told us so far, anybody. So on what authority did you go to Croatia -- excuse me, go to Bosnia and lead these actions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at the beginning, Mr. Prosecutor, that my going to Bosnia was something I did voluntarily. I sought no authorisation to do so, and there was no authorisation. I didn't ask for authorisation from anybody, nor was I able to get it -- nor could I have got it from anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got down there, there were all these soldiers gathered around you, submitting themselves to your command and took part in these very significant military actions. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wish to tell you is that when I arrived in a territory at a given time - and I can tell you during that time, from month to month - I did have the authority of a commander, and I did --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From who? Who gave you the authority as a commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Authority is not something that is given, sir. Somebody either has authority or does not, authority within himself. Whereas, I received authorisation from nobody. And I am repeating that for the third time now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. Just explain that. To help the Chamber with this, how can you just assume authority without any basis for doing so -- having it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which authorisation, Mr. Prosecutor? I take over responsibility, not authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I interrupt. We're going round and round in circles. Could you ask this witness when he went to Bosnia and Herzegovina and took over command of the liberation of Mostar, what was his position in Croatia as assistant minister, what was his position in the Croatian army, had he resigned from those positions, how was he paid, and follow that line of inquiry in short directive questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Judge Clark. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I don't mean that to be critical, but we can go round and round in circles. Because General Praljak, or the former General Praljak, is obviously very emotionally involved and intellectually bound with the position that he's in. And obviously we have to treat him as a person who is a partisan in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Clark, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I should like to add that authority is a situation of fact which evolves juridically, a circular decree, an order. Otherwise you can't just appear on the scene and be imbued with authority, empowered with authority, unless there is a legal basis for that. So could you concentrate your questions on the legal basis, the legal foundations for that authority. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Diarra, thank you. That's exactly what I have been trying to do in response to your question, comment. And in response to Judge Clark, I couldn't -- I fully agree. And in fact those questions -- those very questions are in my outline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So sir, we will just proceed that way. So when you went to Herceg-Bosna to do these -- carry out these actions, were you still a member of the army of the Republic of Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the Ministry of the Republic of Croatia who voluntarily was leaving that post and going to another state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's part of the question. That's a different answer to a different question. But were you still an officer in the Republic of Croatia army, the HV?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the rank of an HV and was an officer of the HV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your rank at that time, was it correct, as we saw earlier, major general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you carry any other rank or title or position other than Major General in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Down there I did not have a rank. Down there I had just the command -- just command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you paid during this time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In different ways. Sometimes through the HVO and sometimes, if I was in Zagreb, through the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you were served -- when you liberated Mostar, who were you being paid by?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an exact answer to that question for that particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you liberated Capljina, who were you being paid by?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about two months, I received my salary down there in the south. And as to the rest, I couldn't give you an exact answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You received a salary from whom or what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the institution representing the Department of Finance of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where the HVO was getting its money at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From many sources. In view of the fact that it wasn't a state, in view of the fact that it was an -- the organised people. In view of the fact that that was the beginning of the -- a minimum degree of organisation, the money arrived from hundreds of thousands of people living abroad as aid and assistance. It was coming in from the taxes that the HVO had probably succeeded in raising on oil, petroleum, and other high tariff goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you indicating -- excuse me, sir, but are you indicating that you -- what you just said a moment ago, that a non-state -- a non-state was collecting taxes to finance the war effort?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "from states," then it's just like me saying -- when we say the difference between a child -- a still unborn child and an adult, a fully grown man. And the road travelled -- that is to say, the beginning of something which over the next 20 years will become a state in the organisational sense of the word. That is the path traversed. So unfortunately, the answer to that question of yours, the question of when inception took place, when a man was conceived -- is a child an adult because it has all the adult's -- all the attributes of a future man, of a future adult? I don't want to complicate the issue, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, as evidence of -- I'll let the Chamber decide whether that -- judge for itself whether that is a responsive answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We are at the break I understand too. Maybe we should take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Bring the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Scott. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, throughout 1992, whenever you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you continued to be a senior officer in the army of the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I was in Croatia, and then I was a high-ranking officer in the army of the -- of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is whenever you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, throughout that time period, you continued as an HV officer, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Prosecutor, I wasn't an HV officer but a volunteer who went there of his own volition because my mother -- my mom and dad were in Mostar, because my uncle was in Mostar, because my sister and her husband were in Sarajevo, because in Capljina, next to the barracks, my second uncle lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you resign, then -- are you telling this Chamber that whenever you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina during 1992, you resigned from the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not resign, because the Croatian army tolerated departures and the struggle against evil in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us in your direct examination that there were a couple of times when you happened to say the United States found out about the presence of Croatian units or at least the alleged presence of Croatian units in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on both occasions objected; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to the United States of America. I have never been to the United States of America, nor could I -- nor did I ever make such a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness never said before this Court that he had been to the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. It's not on the question. It was never -- it's not in the question and it wasn't the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe there is some misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll say it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified during your direct examination that there were at least two separate occasions when some representative of the United States government objected to the presence or alleged presence of HV forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the direct examination, the witness testified only about two cases, not at least two cases, to avoid any misunderstandings in the interpretation, repeatedly the witness said, when I asked him, on only two occasions when the HV presence was referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... referred to two cases, two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On two occasions, sir, the American government objected; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. What do you mean by "the American government"? But I quoted the exact name of the man who came from the Embassy of the United States of America in Zagreb, and it was a Mr. Zorelis, who objected to the presence of the Croatian army in April 1992, on the 12th of April. And I will repeat, it was 164 men who had come to a specific area. And I described it next to Medjugorje in Herzegovina, Tepcici and Slipcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you any of that information. You've already testified in direct examination. My question was quite simple, I think . And the Chamber has counselled me about asking simpler questions, which I understand. And my question was very simple. On two occasions, a representative of the United States government objected to the presence of Croatian forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A representative of the Embassy of the United States of America in Zagreb. I do not know who is the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a responsive answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why, Your Honours, I believe it is all very simple. The witness is testifying about a man that he talked with, and he's trying to say that he has no idea what is the American government or whose representative. He's talking about the man whom he saw. And he repeated where that man came from and what his name was. I think this is very simple. He cannot answer any hypothetical questions of the Prosecutor. He says I received the objection of Mr. Zorelis and he came on behalf of the embassy, and he testified twice about that. Oh, excuse me. I'm very sorry. I was too fast. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you really shouldn't answer for your witness. Mr. Praljak, as he keeps telling us, is a very well-educated man and he's well able to answer questions. If he's avoiding the question, then we'll step in. He appears to be deliberately avoiding answering the question. Mr. Praljak, were you aware that a representative of the United States government complained on two occasions about the presence of Croatian troops in Herzegovina? That's a simple question. Were you aware that the government of the United States by whatever way complained to the government in Zagreb about the presence of Croatian troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really want to answer that question, but all I can say is that those were people from the American Embassy. And I really cannot say American government. I do not know any further links between the American Embassy and the state department. I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Judges of this Court are sufficiently aware about the kind of relation that exists between embassies and governments; and therefore, I think we can move on with regard to this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sir, in 1993, I put it to you that by that time, your status in the Croatian army had become - and others - had become more of an issue. And is it correct, sir, that on about the -- give me one moment. I'm sorry - in June 1993, you were granted official leave from the army of the Republic of Croatia? And I would direct your attention to Exhibit 458.2. It should be the next -- I may in the interest of time have to skip a few exhibits. But if you go down one exhibit or two, I believe you'll come to Exhibit 458.2. If you see that document, sir -- again, in the interests of time, do you agree with that document? Do you agree that that in fact states what happened in connection with your request for departure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. What this document says is correct, and I agree with the document. It is truthful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But sir, at no time prior to the 15th of June, 1993 had you ever previously departed from the HV or your HV rank, had you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As officially as this? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to skip Exhibit 534.1, except simply to point it out to the Chamber that it is the -- recognises -- it's communication about the appointment of this man to command of the HVO main staff. It's true, isn't it, sir, that around the 15th of July, 1993, you, at least formally, became again, as we have discussed earlier today, the senior or chief military officer of the HVO; correct? As reflected in part by the communication by General Petkovic? I guess we didn't skip it. Sorry, Mr. President, maybe we should just confirm that. Is that correct, sir? 534.1.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I ask you to go, then, to 578.1, I simply ask you, can you inform the Chamber as to why, on about the 1st of September, 1993, you were removed from a committee, the State Commission for UNPROFOR and the PMEZ? Why were you removed from that committee or commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot answer that. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And would you then go, please, to Exhibit 654.2? Is that a document, sir, by which you, on the 20th of October, 1993, requested reinstatement to the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct, and there is my full signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, with that in mind, let me go back then to the questions we talked about earlier today. Can you just please try one more time to tell what was your status on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina between January of 1993 and your appointment to chief of the HVO in approximately mid-July, 1993? What position or authority did you have in Bosnia-Herzegovina during that period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For reasons that I already stated, my departures were voluntary. I had no official appointment at -- in that regard, I had no official responsibility and duty. I went there whenever I could to help in the defence of the integrity and the rescue of lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can't help the Chamber with any more understanding as when you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina in January, 1993, and led the attack on Gornji Vakuf, on what position you held at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an attack on Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to mince words with you on that at this particular moment. During the action, during the armed conflict that took place around Gornji Vakuf in January, 1993, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I enjoyed no official position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your de facto position, sir? You commanded the HVO troops in that action, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was helping the commander of that action in everything, both by virtue of the respect that I commanded, I therefore also enjoyed the commanding powers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you don't remember being interviewed by the BBC and saying in that interview that you, Slobodan Praljak, commanded the HVO action at Gornji Vakuf in January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well that BBC's programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you admitted or you stated in that interview --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I still say that officially that was not the case, but that simply because of the respect that I commanded, I had the commanding power. Not denying it, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're telling this Chamber, then, sir, is that one can have very substantial de facto power and authority whether one has a formal rank or not? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself are telling this Chamber that you led men in battle, commanded armed engagements, without any formal title, rank or position; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain, yes, strictly specified actions, yes. For the simple reason that it was an armed people there, with very little of what a normal army would consider an organisation, a system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me, sir. We have to move forward. In Mostar, in May, 1993, when you were there, did you have a formal position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness be allowed to finish his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. I think that the witness has already finished his answer. Did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was about to go on and the Prosecutor interrupted him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, did you finish your answer to the question put forward by the Prosecution? If not, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One needs to understand what it means, an armed people, and absence of the organisational forms of a state, if one is to understand what it means to assume personally the responsibility and what authority or rather the respect one can command mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina between January and the middle of July, 1993, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always placed myself under the command of the Chief of the Main Staff, General Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during that time, you're telling the Chamber that Milivoj Petkovic was your superior commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I endeavoured to act always in line with, and I listened to, and we consulted with General Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were your subordinates? I asked you about your superior. My question now is who were your subordinates during that first six and a half month period in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that for the first six months of 1993, I spent that whole time in Bosnia-Herzegovina? But I was not there all the time during the first half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to argue with you about that right now. When you were there -- listen to my question, please. When you were there in the first six and a half months of 1993, who were your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, when I was there, then my subordinates were only those who would at that particular point in time come to that front line, ready to fight, just as I was ready to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were a very senior commander. You seem willing to use the term "commander." You were a very senior commander. Now in most military organisations, even those that are relatively ill organised, senior commanders have deputy commanders and people that they act through and with. Who did you -- who were your immediate subordinates that you acted through and with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Former commanders in well-regulated armies have precisely specified forms of responsibility and command. In my case, Mr. Prosecutor - I will repeat - I was the commander of only those men who at that moment, together with me, in a certain area defending their part of the turf against the aggressor, as a combatant and as a commander and in a manner in which, as you could see, I had to take a stance. Even though I was a commander of the HVO, I nevertheless had to climb APCs. And that, I think, is unimaginable in the case of some American general or the commander of the 101 Marine Division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll disagree with you about that. But name one person. You said on the times -- all the things you've just said. When you were in the field on some particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I didn't really understand the answer. I do not know whether it was an interpretation problem or what. About climbing what? I didn't really get that part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I climbed the APC to let the convoy through. I was the commander of the entire HVO. And it is unimaginable in a well-organised army such as the Prosecutor is referring to -- it is unimaginable that such a role could be played by a commander of a brigade, let alone a commander of an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Diarra, does that assist you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, again, I don't want to argue about that. I think any number of armies could tell stories about senior officers doing very brave things in combat. But the point of it is this: Name one of these subordinates. Just name one.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wherever you were, sir. You said that you in the first six and a half months --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll use that one.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Realtime transcript read in error "Ian Smith"] Jurgen Schmidt, a Croat with a German surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That came across in the transcript as "Ian Smith," sir. So perhaps you could spell that, if you will.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Ian. "J" -- Jurgen, Jurgen -- Deutsch, German. J-U -- with an umlaut -R -- and Schmidt, Jurgen Schmidt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you name another one? How about in Mostar in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar, in May -- 1992 you mean. Do you mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I mean May 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't remember being in Mostar in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, maybe we'll get to Mostar in May 1993 eventually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Just to go to basics. In 1992 when General Praljak was a general in the Croatian army, and he said that he went to Croatia as a volunteer --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: To Bosnia, sorry, as a volunteer. Who did he report to? Who did he volunteer? How did he know where to go? Let's go back to very basic questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, my apology. I asked -- I think the record will show that I asked exactly that question and never did get an answer. But perhaps he'll be more responsive to your question, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, do you mind if I pose the question, because normally we wait till the very end of cross-examination and re-examination. But sometimes the questions are so out of context, it just opens a whole new arena. So forgive me if I ask this question now. When you left Croatia and you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina -- I think we understand fully that the problem at the time was the Serb and Montenegrin aggression and that you, as you told us, as a person with very strong family contacts in Bosnia-Herzegovina felt a loyalty, a duty, and an ethical duty to go and do something. You said that you went as a volunteer. Who did you report to when you volunteered? I mean, when one goes as a volunteer, you just don't turn up in a town and take over a command. There might be somebody there already in command. So obviously there were a few steps that you had to go through before you arrived at somebody who was respected as a de facto commander. And we're curious about that. Who did you actually go to and report your presence to when you first volunteered in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would take my car in Zagreb or somewhere else. At times, I'd take my weapon with me in the boot of the car; at times I would go without it. And then upon arriving down there, I'd report to the command, to General Petkovic, and ask him, "Well, where are the problems? Where is it difficult? Where is the trouble? Where's the fire?" And if I went without a rifle, then in Gruda, I would be issued with a rifle, change the uniform if -- that is, if there were any uniforms, go to a particular area, and there with groups of men from different units try to see what could be done at that particular moment. That is how it was literally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sticking for a moment longer on the first six and a half months of 1993, following up on Judge Clark's question, and again, as asked you earlier, who paid you during the time you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Prosecutor, that I have already answered that question. The exact answer is as follows: My wife received the money that throughout the war I didn't have any need of nor did I see it at all, see any of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't my question, again, sir. I didn't say anything about your wife receiving the money. Where did that money come from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered that question. But let me repeat. Part of the money came from Croatia. As the HVO began to be better organised, so it was able to take on all the forms of financing. It was a poor form of financing, but that was what the times were like and hundreds of other -- from hundreds of other sources as well in something that is called a general national uprising against aggression. It is difficult --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thank you. You've answered my question, and I do have to go on. Was there a time during any of your time -- let me strike that. During any of the time that you spent in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether in 1992 or 1993, was Zelkjo Siljeg ever one of your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what circumstances? Was he a deputy? Was he an immediate kind of aide de camp? A deputy to you? Was he a brigade commander? How was he subordinate to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zelkjo Siljeg was commander of the operative zone from Tomislavgrad to Bugojno and Konjic, and later left that operative zone in 1992. At that time, in that territory, I spent quite some time, from the fall of Jajce in April, right up until the end of 1992, reinforcing and strengthening the front line towards the Serbs and developing cooperation with the Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a direct subordinate to you? By that I mean without any intermediate officers or commanders, did he report -- when you became the chief officer of the HVO, did he take orders from you and report to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My direct subordinate was the head of the Main Staff of the HVO. Brigadier Tole was his name. And it was through him, when I was commander of the HVO, that correspondence took place with the zone commanders, that we corresponded with the zone commanders. At that time, 1993, from June until October, he was not my direct subordinate, my immediate subordinate. There was a level in between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was Mr. Tole, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zarko Tole, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to go back for a moment. My colleague has indicated in the transcript, I think this name should be correct, Zeljko Siljeg. The spelling is - and I'll ask the witness to confirm if this is true. I believe the spelling is Z-e-l-j-k-o, S with a diacritic, i-l-j-e-g.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Zeljko Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Siljeg was another one of these men who had come from the HV to take on a senior role in the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Siljeg came from the Yugoslav People's Army. He had come from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recall him being in the 115th HV Brigade prior to coming to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I don't know that. But I do know that he was born in Ljubusko and that is where his family lives. It's in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember General Bobetko appointing Zeljko Siljeg on the 14th of July, 1992, to commander of the Tomislav Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, the commander, the Chief of Staff of the HVO, was Milivoj Petkovic. General Bobetko wrote out his orders and distributed them without any real links with reality, although as a co-fighter in the antifascist struggle during World War II and a general of the Yugoslav People's Army and an elderly man, he was listened to, people listened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apparently except you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a little tougher, harder, precisely because I considered that there ought to be more law and order and less personal, putting oneself forward personally on paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall -- do you recall yourself, on the 12th of November, 1992, addressing a letter to Ivan Cermak, who you identified earlier as a senior HV officer, requesting for Siljeg to coordinate salary for the regulations of the ministry of the Republic of Croatia and to pay the remaining amount? Do you remember sending that letter to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that, but if you show it to me, I will certainly testify to its authenticity, if it is indeed authentic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also then don't recall saying in that same letter that Siljeg was registered in the 115th HV Brigade at that time? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how many other senior HV officers were there similar to you and Mr. Siljeg --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just like I myself in the cross-examination, when I claimed something, you would draw my attention to the fact that I should show the documents. So I now ask the Prosecutor to show us that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have that letter available at your hands, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not in my hand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because I didn't make every single piece of paper an exhibit, Your Honour, or this binder would be much bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe it's an important letter, since you come across this issue during your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, I'll seek to make it available to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this answer allows me to say that then this is trying to trip the witness up, an attempt to trip up the witness, and I was cautioned, when I conducted my cross-examination, but if proceedings evolve in this way, then I can safely say that they are trying to trip the witness up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me respond, please, to that briefly. That is not correct. The Chamber will know - particularly Judge Clark, I think, will know - that response -- the responsibility of counsel is to put questions for which there is a good-faith basis to do so. I have done that. And I can and I will seek to provide that document to the Chamber. But I can put facts -- I submit respectfully I can put facts to this witness and see if he agrees or not. He either remembers -- if he doesn't know and he doesn't remember, he can say so. There is no requirement that I put every piece of paper in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Scott, as you know, you've now been challenged by the Defence to say, "Produce this document." And in normal circumstances, you ought to be in a position to produce it. And also the witness has said to you, "If you show me the document, I might be able to see if I recall the contents." So I think in fairness -- obviously, you're going to be in trouble with us if, as Mr. Krsnik alleges, that you were setting a trap. That's not allowed. If the document exists and it says what you say, and I trust you that it does, then, yes, what you're doing is correct. But once the witness has asked for an opportunity to see the document, and Mr. Krsnik is suspicious about the bone fides of the document, in fairness, you should produce it. But I appreciate that, you know, you have a lot of documents, but the President did say to you if you thought it was important enough to cross-examine the witness on it, you should have had the document in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Mr. President and Judge Clark, I appreciate that. I'll seek to make that document available before the -- this witness is concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one second more. I should like to see the order, the alleged order, of the 28th of July, for full combat readiness for Stolac. The situation is the same, is identical, from the beginning of the cross-examination. When we asked where the order was, could we see it, we didn't get it. We weren't shown it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will seek to do that, Your Honour. I guess I must say that, perhaps if the Court will allow me to defend myself for one moment, there does seem to be a difference in practice. I'll certainly abide by the practice here, but not consistent with the practice where I come from. But I will seek to make both those documents available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution has promised to bring those documents so I think this matter is over. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my last question to you before the objection was, how -- is it correct, then, that there were a number of senior HV officers who went back and forth to Herceg-Bosna, the same as you and Mr. Siljeg? For instance, was the same true for Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As did many others too, from that territory, who had families like I did. And the correct answer is, I don't know, when you say larger number, ten, 15, 20, then I can give you a more precise answer, but, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying as to Mr. Petkovic, yes? Do I have your answer correctly, yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ante Roso?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Miljanko Crnjec? And forgive me if I say that incorrectly, Miljanko Crnjec?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miljanko Crnjec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miljanko, M-i-l-j-a-n-k-o, Miljanko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Was he one of these senior HV officers who went to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, yes, at the very beginning, that is to say in April, 1992, he, for a brief, limited period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zdravko -- excuse me again, Z-d-r-a-v-k-o Andabak, not to be confused with Ivan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdravko Andabak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he another one of those senior HV officers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he replaced me in Mostar, in 1992, in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Miro Andric? Was he a senior HV officer who went to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miro Andric, born in Bijelo Polje by Mostar, came as a volunteer. He went down there voluntarily, after the Chetniks had burnt his village and killed more than 20 people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he go, sir -- did he go there being, having been and continuing to be, a senior HV officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He continued to be Miro Andric there with a command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that from the beginning of the HVO in April 1992 at least until the end of 1993, every senior commander, every -- well, by senior commander -- excuse me - the top commander, the person you became in the middle of July 1993 -- everyone who held that position had been a senior HV officer and continued to be? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Many of them, like myself, went for longer or shorter periods of time and later went to the Croatian army to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question, please. And we'll take as long on this as we have to today. You said that Milivoje Petkovic was the senior officer, if I heard you correctly, in 1992 and in the first six and a half months of 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Milivoje Petkovic left the Croatian army as soon as he joined the HVO -- came to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that -- as opposed to me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as the Chamber has reminded me to do. Milivoje Petkovic, whatever else you want to say about him, was the - you're telling us, if I've understood your testimony - the top HVO commander, the position of -- the equivalent of the position you took later, in 1992 and the first six and a half months of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Petkovic came from being a very senior officer in the HV, did he not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did come. And before that, he was the commander of the Sibenik Brigade. But I think that Mr. Petkovic had -- said that he would like to be relieved of his duties in the Croatian army in April 1992, that he did that in 1992, just as I did in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, sir, you became from approximately mid-July 1993 until - you tell us - late October, sometime in November 1993, you were the chief of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave that position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, approximately, sir. Mid-November 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the middle. I handed over duty on the morning of the day when the old bridge in Mostar was destroyed. Two days before that was the beginning of the takeover and assumption of duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps we'll come back to that again later. But in any event, then, if the old bridge was destroyed on approximately the 9th of November, 1993, it was around that time that you ceased being the chief commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not approximately but exactly. On the morning -- on that morning, I signed with General Roso, who came after me, a paper on the taking over of duty. Two days before that, I was relieved of my duties as the main commander of the HVO. And for two days this handing over of duty took place. It lasted for two days. And at 9.00 -- or rather, 8.30 on that morning, I set out for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person who took over this top position was Ante Roso; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also came from the HV. A senior officer in the HV, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a senior officer, first of all, of the Foreign Legion of the French army from where he had -- came to Croatia first of all to defend his homeland, Croatia, and then later on his second homeland, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did Mr. Roso stay in that position as the head -- as the chief commander of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask Mr. Roso that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no idea, sir, you're telling this Chamber that you can assist us with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could be of assistance to the Chamber, but it would be an approximation. You have the exact dates. The dates exist. So I don't think that either the Trial Chamber or you think that it would be difficult to find documents for an exact date. I -- all I would do would be guessing. It would be guesswork on my part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, don't guess. But give us the approximate date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the witness has already answered that question. Asked and answered. And the witness does not wish to testify secondhand or to make guesses. So I think he answered that question twice, in fact, already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, Mr. Krsnik. He said -- he said he will give an approximate date, not exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then the interpretation was wrong or the transcript was wrong, Your Honour. I have to draw your attention to that. The gentleman in the Croatian language said he did not wish to make approximations, which means he did not want -- wish to hazard a guess. That's what the witness said in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, is that an important issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think this witness should be able to assist the Chamber with that, but I'll move on. It's not -- no, it's not worth stopping over.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know that. Eight years have gone by since then. Mr. Roso came after me. I started doing other things. And it really would be guesswork on my part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, throughout the time period that you were -- that you've told us about today so far, between March 1992 and the time in early November when you ceased being the senior commander of the HVO -- during that time period did you ever cease, stop, being the Assistant Minister of Defence for the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I left the army of the -- left the HV, I ceased to be the Assistant Minister of Defence for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you send some resignation letter to Gojko Susak or somebody or Franjo Tudjman to that effect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A document exists in which I requested that. And we looked at it a moment ago. I requested to be relieved of my duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that was as an HV officer. What you indicated earlier today was perhaps the rank of major general. My question to you now is as the Assistant Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Acting military service at the time including the fact that I would cease to be Assistant Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, aren't there a number of civilians who are Ministers of Defence or Assistant Ministers of Defence? You don't have to be a military person to have that role.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have to, but that's how it was. It wasn't necessary, but it was customary at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you'll give me just a moment. I'm trying to figure out the best way to use the next 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's start this topic today. We probably won't conclude it. But your dealings specifically with the man Mladen Naletilic. You said you were childhood friends; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I've known him since my childhood, that we at times played together, and our relationship can be described as a childhood friendship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer to my question was again yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not too close because he was slightly younger, but in -- in a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time period that you've been talking about primarily in your testimony, from about March 1992 until the end of 1993, can you tell the Chamber, give the Chamber some idea of the extent of your dealings with Mr. Naletilic during that time. Did you see him many times, a dozen times, less than a dozen times in that approximately, let's say, 20-month period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about a dozen times. Yes, I did see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what capacities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned one capacity, concerning the vantage point above Mostar, that is, Orlovac. I saw him twice, I believe, at the time of religious festivals that we mark, around the Assumption Day. I also saw him several times at funerals. I saw him, and I saw his children too. Once I visited him at his place. I also saw him in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you visit him - just now you said "at his place" - at his home in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think only once, sir. Just to see if he'd built his house properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see him -- strike that. How many times did you see him in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe to the Chamber, if you can, the circumstances during which you saw Mr. Tuta twice in Zagreb. Were these meetings that you saw him in, or how did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Both times it was by chance. Once in Jelacic Square, and another occasion I think in a hotel or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw him at Orlovac, in connection with Mostar in, would you agree, approximately June 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. It could have been either the beginning of June or perhaps late May.
